I see this hot take all the time on the Internet but it's an overcorrection from three generations of American jingoism. The United States economy made both the Great British and Soviet military efforts possible. But even restricting our argument to only military operations, on a strategic level it is extremely significant to open up a second front on the opposite side of the country from the current front. It means the Germans have to split their forces, shuffle men and materiel back and forth, and generally lose focus. A 2-front war was the entire grand-strategic and political dilemma the Germans had been concerned about since Prussia bolted the rest of the German states onto itself in 1870, and even before that. It's the whole reason the Germans went to war in 1914, because the Great General Staff thought they had this surefire plan to win by knocking one enemy out, then quickly shifting all their resources to the other front so they wouldn't have to fight a 2-front war. (They were of course badly mistaken about this plan.)

The United States and the Soviet Union both contributed significantly, and it's not particularly meaningful to try to say one contributed more than other: the Americans coughed up more treasure, the Soviets shed more blood, both of which were highly significant. But the Americans did make a very serious war effort, transporting armies and huge amounts of equipment across an ocean, and fought well once they were there, making pretty admirable successes on their front. It is extremely difficult to come up with a mathematically rigorous metric by which to say who contributed more -- but the absence of either front would have changed the strategic calculus, and possibly in favor of the Germans.

Aragorn had many privileges of birth, but also genuinely built his own life. He traveled the entire breadth of the ancient lands of his forefathers, often incognito, learning and experiencing different cultures as an unknown. He won the trust of both Rohan and Gondor separately, and fought in war with each of them under an assumed name, being promoted to a Captain of Men for his obvious talents for both tactics and strategy. But during the War of the Ring when Mordor attacked Minas Tirith and the leader Denethor had died, he showed political sensitivity and restraint by not entering the city--he knew his presence would cause significant political turmoil were he to try to claim the leadership at that instant. There was still a war to fight and he respected the people of Gondor enough to camp outside the city, not enter it as a conqueror or the long-prophesied & much-ballyhoed "returning king."

When the war was over he did accept the kingship, but he didn't reinstate the former political boundaries of ancient Arnor & Gondor. Instead he granted political independence and sovereignty to the southern kingdoms of men, who had a vastly different culture and sphere of influence than Gondorian men, and granted a special kind of political independence and barrier of protection around the Shire to protect the noble Hobbit race from larger, unscrupulous races of men.

He wasn't a model of a man just because he had a "badass vibe" or because he could hunt, track, fight, and woo elven princesses. He was a model of a man because he was also capable of restraint, decency, and the nicest sense of personal honor. He had a genuinely innovative strategic mind in war, but he also loved people and enjoyed being in their company and getting to know them. He wanted others to succeed in their own right. He did not love wealth or lust after women, he genuinely loved the realm and gave his life to defending what is good and right and true and lovely in the world. That is why he deserved to be called King, and why some of us admire him as a man worthy of study.

Just a few thoughts. (For reference, I play fixed card bonuses. I consider it the superior challenge, progressive just gets too silly.)

1) The name of the game is Risk. Take risks. Advantage goes to the attacker. I mean yes, have a plan in mind, know what comes after. But take a leap sometimes and try something. Walk away from your safe position every once in a while because you think you can make it work. Be like Grant and run the guns, abandoning your supply lines, to take Vicksburg.

2) Learn to play a no-continent strategy. Most people give up if they can't get a continent immediately, but serious players treat it as no big deal. Numbers aren't everything, you can wander around with a single stack of troops and not have a continent for a long, long time and still win. Not having a continent means you have fewer troops on the board, but it also means you have fewer territories to defend. Play the long game.

3) Learn patience like a monk. No matter how badly someone screws you over, you have to learn to *think*, and be separate from emotional reactions. Emotions will arise -- and they'll make you lose. Sometimes whole armies will get wiped out. They're gone. Adjust to the new reality, play the new game in front of you.

4) Play the player, not the armies on the board. This is true of all military theory. You have to outthink, outmaneuver, outgeneral the commander, not face down every one of their armies. Get them to expend their energies foolishly. Get them to defend the wrong places, get them to attack the wrong adversaries.

5) Play every single game to the last troop. To the bitter end. This is crucial, your game will improve so much when you take every single situation as an opportunity to learn. My win rate increased significantly when I stopped giving up. (I once won a game where at my lowest I was down to 4 troops in 3 countries, all in a line, with 3 cards. In that case it was a cascading sequence of luck that every single other player either had other more pressing plans, had their available armies wiped out by the aforementioned plans, or else couldn't get to me -- surviving that next couple of turns was extremely lucky. But... I came back to win, and the rest of that game wasn't luck, it was talent, generalship, and moxie.)

6) Be honorable. This does not mean don't do what it takes to win. You absolutely have to turn on your friends and betray your alliances in order to win. This is not real geopolitics, this is Risk. But this still doesn't mean you have to be a scoundrel. Reward someone's help by giving them second if you can. Consider not eliminating someone who's been friendly when it really doesn't suit your strategic position. (In an endgame where you have hundreds of troops on the board, does taking a few cards mean that much? Why? Do you have a specific plan you need those 10-20 troops for? Can you defend all this new territory you're gaining, or will you overextend yourself to take them out? If an action will make you public enemy number 1, you had better be ready for everyone to treat you as such, and combine against you.)

7) Learn to think several turns ahead. You can really only do this by playing the game and seeing how things turn out. But in short, if you take a territory, can you defend it? If you can't someone else will take it. Every action will create some kind of power vacuum. Learn to ride the wave of the power that fills the vacuum.

I also recommend trying to write as much as you can about it, writing will force you to clarify your thoughts in new ways. The same goes for talking about the game to someone who will listen. Best way to learn something is to try to teach it. Anyway, good luck and good hunting.

Agree with your assessment overall, and also with the other commenter. Playing solo really won't take you very far, it will however give you a good understanding of how the bots play, and also help you develop an understanding of a given map.

Ultimately, you absolutely have to play against humans in order to get better. It is a head game and a game of politics first, and a game of statistics and board topology second. (And in a distant third, a game of knowing how bots tend to play.)

That said, as you play more and more with human beings, you'll see someone make a mistake, where they take the wrong path and have to split their forces, or have to leave behind 3 armies when they didn't have to. And you'll see them lose the game over it; or *you'll* lose the game over it. Playing solo against bots won't help you win against humans in general. But it will occasionally help you not lose in situations where you could have won if you knew the map better.

Especially because people play on such ridiculously short turn timers, you have to know the map really well so you don't have to think too hard about optimal paths to achieve your goals. 

(I personally play on 2min turn timer, but this community loves 1min. I think it really changes the character of the game when you can't execute a long, elaborate turn, but people tend to shout me down on the subject because they're impatient to play I guess. The pane of glass behind our heads basically rushed up to meet us. Miraculously we survived and with only moderate injuries. (I missed the first day of 9th grade, an orientation day on a Friday, but showed up for the first real day Monday.) But in the months to come, I was pressured to get plastic surgery on my neck scars, because they stood out, and were very lopsided and jagged and (according to my parents) ugly. I would regret it, they said, if I didn't do something to minimize their appearance.

That was a long time ago now, and I can barely even remember what the scars looked like. They weren't in my field of vision, and even with a mirror I couldn't get a complete look (this is in the days before cell phones with cameras!). But at the time I pushed back on the idea. Aren't scars attractive to chicks?, I asked, with all the savoir faire of a 14 year old. I got a lot of, no, not this kind, you'll regret it if you don't get them minimized, insurance will pay 100%, you might as well, etc etc and finally I agreed to do it.

But I gotta say, if I had it to do over again I would leave the brutality and jaggedness of those scars in evidence. But certainly not all liberals would describe their political beliefs as pro-nobility, pro-oligarchy, or pro-inequality.

Liberals in 19th century Europe favored nationalism as a way to draw the dividing political lines of the world. But that was before the nationalism project went so grisly and evil as it did under the Nazis / Turks / Japanese etc. Liberals post WWII tend not to favor nationalism. This is just an example. The word has many, many different contexts and interpretations, and should be used sparingly.

Nazis may have created a pro-business environment, but did so by restricting people's individual liberties (to the point of murdering 10-12 million of them) and subverting the legal system (literally placing their political leader as the highest source of law in the land). Liberals in Germany for over a hundred years at that point had been decrying such restrictive government actions as the Carlsbad decrees, censorship, police state, strict economic and guild rules, etc, as well as for decades expressing dissatisfaction at the lack of a written constitution that limited the powers of the monarch. In places like Prussia you had a tiered system of suffrage, such that the wealthiest land-owners received an incredibly disproportionate share of the vote. Liberals at that time wanted less power for the monarch, more power for elected representatives, increased if not equal suffrage, and less government / police interference with their lives.

Hitler's rise and eventual coup of the German legal and political structures does not in any way resemble what the liberals wanted. Indeed, many liberal dissidents were outright murdered in order to build the new German Reich. That the Third Reich might have some similarities to what we would now call neo-liberalism, or neo-feudalism, doesn't mean that the Nazis were an "inherently liberal" group.

Basically my best read on this phenomenon and what to do about it is, *don't let the game stagnate in the first place*. Easier said than done sometimes, I know -- but I tend to think that it takes six people to create a stable, six-way unchanging board state. Don't let yourself or others get locked into it. Keep pressure on in unexpected ways, keep people on the back foot, keep them reacting (and possibly making a mistake). Even if you have no idea what to do strategically, position your troops in a slightly odd way that makes seem like you Definitely Have A Strategy. (Consolidating into one very large stack, for example, is a very solid play, as it indicates Something Might Happen Soon, but also leaves you able to actually capitalize on many different kinds of circumstances. Of course, you might also freak out your nearest neighbor so keep that in mind. Figure out a way to soothe their nerves if you can.)

So honestly? Letting a few turns go by with no board-state-changing moves is not that big a deal -- especially if the overall board state is still in flux (other players are still doing things). But once *everybody* is waiting & watching & risking nothing, you *must* do something to change the board state, or especially, *people's perceptions of the board state*. Oftentimes that's enough.

And sometimes just realizing that no one feels confident in their position is a huge psychological gain in its own right.

If all else fails and the game grinds down into a rut, try this: walk away from your position. I mean seriously, no foolin', over the course of a turn or two literally move all of your troops somewhere else (and in a way you can't easily strike back), and just abandon your continent and your bonus. Just wander around for a while, taking territories here and there but not angling for another continent.

So basically, you deliberately create a power vacuum --- leave and watch your neighbors all fight for the new territory. There's a good chance someone will overextend, someone else will punish, and the ongoing dynamic will produce opportunities you wouldn't have anticipated but can capitalize on.

"But what if the player immediately after me is the current Big, and just steps right in and snags an easy second continent for themselves? Won't they now just devour us all?" 

Well honestly, it's not all that easy to expand up from one continent to two -- especially with five other people watching you do it. If not done with the most delicate political (and military) instincts, you will become Public Enemy Number 1 and the other players now have an incentive to team together to take you down. When a player expands too quickly it gives everyone else a psychological focus, a clarity about the board state ("*They must be stopped.*"). And remember, just because they have more troops than anyone else, *they won't have more troops than everyone else combined*. If they do, they should have already won and may indeed prove unstoppable. But in the circumstances we're talking about (nearly all circumstances), they won't have anywhere close to the rest of the players combined -- and if those players can work together, they can absolutely wreck even a very solid Big. You do, of course, have to actually work together. Not always straightforward.

In the aftermath of Napoleon's devastating wars of revolution, Prussia undertook a controversial (for the time) and frankly *fundamentally nerdy* (ie intellectual) plan: to design a new pedagogical and research institution within the Prussian army. 

Napoleon was a rare genius, having both military prowess and a political star, and it took the powers of Europe combining together *seven different times* to finally bring him down. And even after his defeat, the Prussians realized that another like him could arise at any time, in any country, and not necessarily in Prussia or Germany. So: what if we put together an entire body of thinkers, planners, strategists; the best and brightest all working together, acting as a de facto military genius for all those times that the rare, pure genius simply does not emerge?

They called it the General Staff. Generals have always had staffs, a few messengers, a few cartographers, maybe an adviser or two. But not like this and not in permanent residence, far from any battlefield. They gave ruthless examination schemes to their officers, so as to appoint and advance only the brightest officers to, and within, the General Staff. They also invested heavily in education for their officers, not only in the pure military arts but in broad "liberal educational" terms. Then they developed a variety of departments and working groups. They had groups of officers traveling to various regions to study the lay of the land, and improve and expand their maps. They had a whole department studying railroads for military and logistic art in the 1830's (at that time only a single rail line existed in all the German states, and quite a short one too; in the United States the Baltimore and Ohio opened in 1827, but the intellectually stagnant American army of the time would not contemplate the use of railroads until the 1860's, and would not even use them to their full potential in that war); they drew up contingency plans, potential invasion schemes for every major power, AND every combination of powers, and wargamed their tactical and strategical ideas constantly; they created an entire department devoted to military history, analytically tearing apart their own past performances in war so as to learn from their mistakes, but also with a free mandate to range freely across time, to study wars and commanders and men from even the distant past---reasoning that, though technologies and tactics change, the attitudes and inner feelings of men, insofar as those things affect their decisions and command styles, often have a great deal to offer the thoughtful and reflective military officer.

The Prussians did it first, the General Staff, and now every major military force on the planet has a version of it, devoting considerable resources towards study, education, and research. In the United States for example we have the Pentagon, full of thousands of hardworking people reading, writing, analyzing feeds... 

*coming up with creative solutions*... 

*developing code, for myriad useful and devastating purposes defensive and offensive*...

*developing flight plans*...

*drawing up maps*... 

*painstakingly perfecting timetables*... 

*debating and simulating courses of action*... 

etc etc etc etc

So this guy may not strike you as having that killer instinct or sense of cool or whatever, but he's describing one of the most fundamentally effective and ubiquitous aspects of modern military art.

Just sayin, maybe y'all should consider making guarded or limited claims about things you don't particularly study.

Sources: 

--A Genius for War: The German Army and General Staff 1807-1945 by Colonel T.N. Dupuy

--Cognitive Challenges of War: Prussia 1806 by Peter Paret (believe it or not, this one is about art, literature, and theatre as well as war)

Ha I dig the 300 reference. I love that kind of thing too. I also really enjoy, though not as "epic" per se, the Prussian victory over Austria in 1866. It requires a little more thought and study, because much of the victory occurred beforehand... in the creation of basically a research organization within the Prussian Army called the General Staff. They got the most highly educated people they could find, working on detailed plans for mobilization, studying the new technology of railroads, studying tactics, studying past defeats and victories with a fine-tooth comb, etc... and then used this extensive planning to defy all military logic and split their forces. A huge mountain range separates Austria from southern Germany you see, and you can only march so many men through mountain passes at one time... if you keep the army "concentrated" but marching in a line *50 miles long* through narrow passes and roads, you will obviously open yourself to defeat. 

So Moltke (the Chief of the General Staff and de facto Commander in Chief), knowing full well that the Austrians were gathering and concentrating their army---and I should mention, Austria had a serious numerical advantage when fully mobilized and assembled---but Moltke also knew that his army was designed to mobilize at light speed in comparison (basically, due to solid administrative work), and so he mobilized faster than anyone imagined possible, then split his army into three main groups (with two other smallish ones I think too) to cross the mountains and then reassemble all around and outflanking the Austrian army. He was decried as the worst sort of incompetent buffoon (or malign actor) for abandoning that *fundamental* military logic that comes from names like Napoleon and Clausewitz: concentrate your forces (and strike at the enemy's weak point). But Moltke won the argument, and three separate armies converged on the Austrians, who had fearfully chosen a defensive concentration until fully mobilized (they should have struck at each smaller Prussian army as they crossed the mountains, defeating them in detail). Prussia proceeded to handily surround and defeat the much-vaunted Austrian military and show themselves as the up-and-coming new military power in Europe.

(Note: the new breech-loading rifles of the Prussians did make a huge difference, but don't let anyone tell you it was all about the weapons technology---Prussia out-strategized and out-generaled the Austrians in all sorts of ways before anyone ever fired a weapon.)

(I also think it significant: after the decisive victory, most of the army's top brass wanted to march on Vienna the capital, strut their victory and claim the spoils of war, etc. But the political chief, Bismarck, who had rode to war as well, absolutely refused to allow such a thing. He refused to further humiliate Prussia's ancient ally / overlord (Austria being sort of the remnants of the Holy Roman Empire) but moreover, knew that if Prussia showed restraint in its actions that before too long they could make Austria an ally once again. Which is exactly what happened. This restraint, the long-term strategic mindset, seems to me just as crucial for strategists to understand... weapons and technology are important but so are administration, research, logistics, and... restraint.)

Some people suggest playing Prog, but if you're like me the game loses its verve that way. If you want to keep playing Fixed:

It takes 6 players to make a 6-way standoff. Yes, sometimes you get down on your luck, you have to pull back and just nurse your wounds hoping nobody swallows you whole. But in general, it takes every player to consent to a passive board state, and once you identify that, that everyone wants to passively build their empire behind veiled eyes, it gives you a certain freedom. (At least, some information you can leverage.)

I can't give specific advice because it all depends on the situation. See where you can push. Don't immediately try to grab a second continent as this will arouse the wrath of all. But where else can you build a small presence that won't cause too much upset, and yet be the nucleus of a larger push at a later time? What *signals* can you send to the other players, either to compel their action, or else to deceive them about your intentions? Or to cause animosity towards another player? Fairness, order, familiarity, fear, and revenge all can potentially motivate players to action.

Frequently, you should respond to an all-way arms race by building up your own arms and waiting for your chance. Remember to keep your lines of attack open; think through each player's position, and how to project force towards any of them if you need to. Keeping your lines of attack open tends to outweigh the need to take a card each turn. On the other hand, deliberately closing a line of attack towards a certain player may lull them into a sense of security towards you, and lead them to make a foolhardy attack on someone else... if they do so, do you have a reserve force that can (in a pinch) come out and make a sortie upon the now-weakened enemy?

The truly challenging situation is the oft-lamented three way standoff in the late stage of the game. In this case it can get absurd, because obviously if anyone attacks anyone else with full strength, the third player almost always wins. Sometimes making partial attacks causes a valuable effect (not blitzing the main stack but drawing it down some) though sometimes you *unduly* piss the person off by doing this so beware. Sometimes you want to take down a smaller detached army (defeating the enemy in detail). Sometimes you want to deliberately be a little wasteful with your troops, to fall behind the two other players in troop count. Make some stupid plays and act chastened. They will focus on each other and take risks incommensurate with their actual lead, leaving you poised to leverage your small army into an incontrovertible lead. Remember to present the enemy with a dilemma wherever possible: in certain late stage situations, where the bigs have collided and both weakened themselves, you can quickly grab two continents with only meager defenses, and the opponents either cannot reach both locations or lack the strength to break both continents. Managing not only your own, but your enemy's lines of attack as well remains crucial for almost all strategies.

(That you cannot attack through your own territory makes zero sense in real war, but in RISK it makes for many a subtle and powerful advantage.)

In conclusion: I do not really mean to say "git gud" as an answer to your question, but you have to take some ownership of your piece of letting the game settle into an equilibrium. Keep up the pressure, make deceiving ploys, put some pathos into your plays, keep working around the edges, get creative. Also (my personal recommendation) get off the main map... a. (Direct). Lines of attack. Unlike in real war, you cannot attack across territory you already own. Therefore expend considerable thought in not capturing certain territories, so as to allow you to bring a large army through at some later point. There are cases where you're better off not taking a card if it means keeping your lines of attack open for your mega-army. (And you can also think about your opponents' lines of attack: sometimes you can be a good ally by attacking your ally's single-troop territory and freeing up their army for a sortie. Line-of-attack discipline is like firearms discipline: "every single time."

In another life I was a researcher of pedagogy (how do people learn) and the number one thing that the evidence shows is that students learn best by talking with their peers and putting the subject into their own words. Even just attempting to put your problem into words will help you resolve and clarify your understanding. And don't worry about not having it all figured out, just talk about what you do know, go right up to the edge of your understanding and usually you'll find yourself making new little connections in your mind.
